questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069903/assets/4fce9c5eebc7b439d9851ed0ed20df2e0879161b754d63fcd31502b26a8fb82e.png)

 

A thin layer of fluid flows over a certain region of the plane, as shown above. The corresponding velocity vector field is given by $V(x,y)={x}^{2}y\,i+2xy\,j.$

Current part:

The divergence $\text{div}\,V$ of the velocity field represents the scalar rate of expansion of the fluid per unit of area at a given point. Find the corresponding expansion rate at the point $(1,1).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        The required rate of expansion is $\text{div}\,V\,{|}_{(1,\,1)}=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
If $V=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $V$ all exist, then the divergence of $V$ is given by

$$
∇\cdot V=\text{div}\,V=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,V & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy) \\  & =2xy+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,V$ at the point $(1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,V\,{|}_{(1,\,1)} & =2(1)(1)+2(1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\text{div}\,V) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+2x) \\  & =2y+2 \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(\text{div}\,V) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+2x) \\  & =2x+0 \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

    

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\text{div}\,V)\,{|}_{(1,\,1)} & =2(1)+2 \\  & =4 \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(\text{div}\,V)\,{|}_{(1,\,1)} & =2(1) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}(-3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

In part 3, we found that the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ is

$$
∇\,f(1,1)=∇(\text{div}\,V)\,{|}_{(1,\,1)}=4\,i+2\,j.
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(4\,i+2\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{5}(-3\,i+4\,j)) \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 4}{5} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

In part 1, we found that 

$$
f(1,1)=\text{div}\,V\,{|}_{(1,\,1)}=4.
$$

And from part 3, we know that the gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ is given by

$$
∇f(1,1)=∇(\text{div}\,V)\,{|}_{(1,\,1)}=⟨4,\,2⟩.
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =4+⟨4,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =4+4(x-1)+2(y-1) \\  & =4x+2y-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

The scalar curl of a plane velocity field is called the **vorticity,** denoted $\omega .$ The vorticity describes a measure of the local rotation of the field at a given point. Find the vorticity of $V$ at $(1,1).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\omega (1,1)=$

questions.worked_solution:
If $V=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $V$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $V$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $P={x}^{2}y$ and $Q=2xy.$ Therefore, the scalar curl (i.e., the vorticity) of $V$ at $(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\omega  & =\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y) \\  & =2y-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\omega (1,1) & =(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,{|}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =2(1)-(1)^{2} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
